newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Fraser hands the RBA reins over to Macfarlane.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Fraser hands the RBA reins over to Macfarlane.

text.p: Bernie Fraser walks out the glass doors the Reserve Bank of Australia in Sydney's Martin Place for the last time as governor on Tuesday leaving an institution which has changed markedly in under his seven years at the helm.
Those changes will continue under his successor, Ian Macfarlane, following the formalisation with the government of the RBA's inflation objective that Fraser introduced.

Macfarlane, who was one of Fraser's two deputy governors, issued a joint statement with the Treasurer, Peter Costello, on the conduct of monetary policy when his appointment for a seven year term was announced by Costello last month.
Under Fraser's tenure, the RBA introduced a target of maintaining the underlying inflation rate to an average of two to three percent over the course of a cycle.
The underlying rate removes volatile and seasonal factors from the consumer price index.

"One of the big successes behind Bernie Fraser was he had that consistent message of underlying inflation, wages and productivity," said Akis Haralabopoulos, chief economist for funds manager GIO Australia.
"That's one reason why he played such an important role in delivering Australia a low inflation environment," he said.
The agreement between Macfarlane and Costello sought to formalise the independence of the RBA in terms of monetary policy, and maintained the RBA's charters multiple objectives.

Those objectives, contained in the Reserve bank Act, are the stability of the currency of Australia, the maintainance of full employment in Australia, and the economic prosperity and welfare of the people of Australia.
"The first two objectives lead to the third, and ultimate, objective of monetary policy and indeed economic policy as a whole," the statement said.
Fraser has always been in favour of the multiple objectives of the RBA's charter, and believes the inflation only focus of many central banks is too limiting.
"It is the job of central banks to worry about inflation, and they are innately inclined to to do that," Fraser said in a speech at the National Press Club in August.
"But they should not be fixated solely with inflation, and we should not be loading the dice even more in that direction."

When Fraser assumed office in September 1989, official interest rates were up near 17 percent, the consumer price index stood at 7.9 percent, underlying inflation was 5.7 percent and the unemployment rate was 6.1 percent.
Cash rates rose to around 18 percent later that year, but in January 1990, Fraser began to cut official interest rates.

With that first move, Fraser introduced the practice of the RBA telling the market not only that it would deal to change the level of interest, but also by how much it intended to change rates and the reasoning behind the move.
Interest rate were reduced on 15 seperate occasions between January 1990 and July 1993, when they troughed at 4.75 percent.
Three increases between August and December 1994 took them back to 7.5 percent, where they remained until July 31 this year, when a cut of 0.5 percentage points was was announced.
Fraser leaves office with offical cash rates at 7.0 percent, the consumer price index and underlying inflation both at 3.1 percent, and an unemployment rate of 8.8 percent.

Under Fraser's governorship, the RBA assumed a more visible public role through both speeches and releases. The January 1990 bulletin contained six pages of reports on financial markets and recent economic news -- by July this year the RBA's quarterly economic report in the bulletin was 22 pages long.
Fraser also began appearing before a parliamentary committee after the release of the RBA's annual report.

Under Macfarlane's agreement with the government, this process will continue, as the RBA will now release six monthly statements on monetary policy and the role it is playing in achieving the RBA's objectives.
As well, Macfarlane will report twice a year on monetary policy before an open parliamentary hearing.
